questions.q: What does Cosmos DB's default indexing policy do?
options: Automatically indexes every property of every item, using the '/*' wildcard include path
Indexes nothing until you manually create an index
Only indexes the partition key
Only indexes properties explicitly marked as 'searchable'
questions.explain: The default policy's includedPaths is just '/*' — every property is indexed automatically, a genuine reversal of the relational default.

questions.q: Why would a team choose to exclude paths from a container's indexing policy?
options: To reduce the request unit (RU) cost of writes and index storage, for properties they never filter or sort on
Because Cosmos DB requires you to exclude at least one path
To make reads faster on the excluded properties
Excluding paths has no real effect on cost or performance
questions.explain: Every indexed property adds RU cost to writes; excluding paths you never query against is a deliberate cost optimization.

questions.q: What happens when you query on a property whose path has been excluded from the indexing policy?
options: The query falls back to a full container scan for that path
The query fails immediately with an error
Cosmos DB automatically re-indexes the property on the fly
The property becomes unreadable
questions.explain: Excluding a path is a real tradeoff — cheaper writes, but a query filtering on that path scans instead of using an index.

questions.q: When is a composite index needed in Cosmos DB?
options: When a query needs an ORDER BY across multiple properties, or a filter on one property combined with a sort on another
For every single-property equality filter
Only when using the MongoDB API
Composite indexes are created automatically for every container and never need configuration
questions.explain: A single-property range index can't efficiently serve a multi-property sort or filter+sort combination — that requires an explicit composite index.

questions.q: How does Cosmos DB's default indexing behavior fundamentally differ from a relational database like SQL Server?
options: SQL Server requires you to explicitly create indexes for columns you want fast queries on; Cosmos DB indexes everything automatically unless you exclude it
There is no real difference — both index every column by default
SQL Server also indexes every column automatically
Cosmos DB never allows any customization of indexing behavior
questions.explain: This is the core distinction the lesson makes: Cosmos DB's default is opt-out indexing, the opposite of the relational opt-in default.
